definition: Pragmatic means guided by what actually works in practice rather than by theories or ideals.
task: Write one sentence of your own using the word pragmatic. Make the sentence show what the word means -- a reader who did not know pragmatic should be able to work it out from your sentence.
avoid_verbatim: The pragmatic captain abandoned the record attempt at the first ice warning; a finished voyage, she said, beats a famous one.
Sensible is milder than pragmatic: a sensible choice merely avoids obvious folly, while a pragmatic one goes further and deliberately trades the ideal answer for the one that will work.
Expedient goes further than pragmatic — the pragmatic mayor bends an ideal to get results, but the expedient one drops the principle entirely if that speeds the outcome.

Practical is the everyday twin — focused on what can be done with the tools at hand. Pragmatic adds a strategist's edge: it's practical as a policy, deliberately ranking what works above what would be ideal.
Realistic is about seeing: a realistic view takes the situation as it actually is. Pragmatic is about doing — the word for choices that act on that clear view and let results decide.

designing for a perfect world that practice can't deliver

When the water grant finally arrived, half the committee wanted the solar pumping array — silent, modern, gleaming in the brochures.
Ines, the committee's pragmatic chair, priced the replacement parts, counted the certified technicians within a hundred miles (two), and asked what happened in the rainy season.
Then she ordered simple hand pumps the village blacksmith could strip and fix by lunchtime.
Ten years on, every one of them still pours.
Pragmatic is the word for Ines because her test for every option was the same: will it work here, for us, and keep working?
Not the most inspiring choice, not the most modern — the one that pours in year ten.
Notice the word passes no judgment on ideals themselves; it just refuses to let them outrank results.
The brochure was beautiful.
level-headed / faintly admiring
Pragmatic is praise with its sleeves rolled up: it credits someone with ranking results above ideals, and only lightly hints at the ideals set aside.
This unit's judicious honors the quality of the weighing; pragmatic honors the outcome-first tiebreak.
Push results-worship one notch further — principle dropped for speed — and the honest word turns to expedient.

The engineering club spent September sketching a robot arm with six joints, a camera, and a claw that could rotate like a wrist.
In October their captain, Dana, ran the numbers: the team had one motor controller, forty hours of build time, and a competition rule that scored only successful lifts.
Her response was pragmatic.
The six-joint arm went into a drawer, and the team built a two-joint lifter that could raise a block every single run.
Some members grumbled that the design felt ordinary next to the original drawings, and Dana agreed that it was.
But the scoreboard, she reminded them, does not award points for the machine you wished you had built.
